title: AlertKick: agent-native website and server monitoring
pitch: Websites and server monitoring that ChatGPT can operate directly on the page. Start with a URL, no agent required. WebMCP exposes website, ssl, domain checks and account specific monitors and alerts.
about_excerpt: Websites and server monitoring that ChatGPT can operate directly on the page. Start with a URL, no agent required. WebMCP exposes website, ssl, domain checks and account specific monitors and alerts. Like Comment Story Updates Listing of WebMCP tools Creating different monitors using the WebMCP Creation of http monitor using webmcp with json output creation of other dns monitor and email monitor Final output of the agent interface after creating all monitors through WebMCP Inspiration I built AlertKick to make monitoring websites and servers dead easy with as little config as possible. In all my previous jobs monitoring and setting up alerting is a lot of moving parts and a lot of config. Even a URL monitoring requires, type a URL, pick an interval, pick a region, pick who gets paged. When something breaks at 3am the person on call then clicks through five more screens to find out what is failing, acknowledge it, and record what they changed. We already run a hosted MCP server so Claude can do all of this over an API key. WebMCP lets the agent already sitting in the user's browser tab do the same thing in the user's own session, with the browser enforcing confirmation on anything risky. That is a much shorter path from "watch my site" to a working monitor, and the user needs nothing except to be logged in. What it does AlertKick monitors websites and servers. Website monitoring needs nothing installed: uptime and response time from multiple regions, TLS certificate and domain expiry, DNS records and cron heartbeats. Teams running their own hosts add the Linux/Windows agent for metrics, Docker and eBPF security detections. Alerts route through on-call scheduling, escalation policies and change control. With WebMCP, two surfaces register their capabilities as page tools: Public free tools at alertkick.com/tools (SSL checker, DNS checker, domain expiry, security headers, website check). Each page registers one read-only tool. "Check the cert on example.com" runs the checker and hands the agent structured JSON instead of a rendered table. The tenant dashboard. On login the app registers the same tool set our hosted MCP server exposes: create and manage HTTPS, TCP, DNS and domain-expiry monitors, heartbeats, list/acknowledge/resolve alerts, inspect servers and containers, and create/approve/start/verify/complete change records. Example flows in the ChatGPT desktop browser: New user with only a URL: "add uptime, DNS and cert-expiry checks for example.com" creates three monitors in one turn. During an incident: "what is paging right now, ack the critical ones and open a change for the fix" becomes list_alerts , acknowledge_alert (confirmed by the user) and create_change . On a free tool page, no account needed: "is example.com's TLS chain valid and when does it expire?" Read tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Every write goes through requestUserInteraction() and the app's own confirm dialog. The agent proposes, a person approves. How it's built One manifest, two tool builds. Our MCP server is written in Go and already defines 34 tools with JSON Schema inputs. A generator dumps name , description and inputSchema to a JSON manifest that the React dashboard imports. The UI supplies only the execute() bodies, each tool is a small call through the same authenticated /api/v1 client which UI already usages. Both MCP and WebMCP share one source of truth, so they cannot drift. Session-scoped registration. Tools register when the auth context resolves a logged-in user and unregister on logout. An unauthenticated tab does not exposes anything. The server side has tenant isolation on every request the same way as for the normal UI calls, so the agent can reach only what the user can. Website tools. I use the same to provide tools on the main site. main site registers per free-tools page via a shared component that wraps the existing /api/tools/* endpoints (Cloudflare rate limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds per IP). Testing. Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and navigator.modelContextTesting.executeTool() for unit-style checks, then end to end in the ChatGPT desktop app against staging and production. Also my MCP server is all tested using MCP Inspector and is also available on the Claude Connectors directory so it's well tested from there as well, and it usages same request parameters. Open source. The manifest generator, registration helper and execute adapters are published as a standalone package so any product with an MCP server can expose it in-page the same way. Challenges we ran into Write safety. A tool that deletes a monitor or approves a change is one sentence away from an accident. Every non-read tool now calls requestUserInteraction() , which opens confirm modal for clicking the button we see. The tool result reports this too, whether the user approved or cancelled. Schema fidelity. Go MCP tool schemas use enums and nested objects that our first manifest export flattened. The generator now emits the schema verbatim and a test asserts the browser manifest equals the server's tools/list response. Spec churn. provideContext() disappeared from the spec in March and the attribute location changed mid-year. We wrote to registerTool / unregisterTool only and kept detection defensive. Registration timing in an SPA. React re-renders and route changes re-registered tools and hit InvalidStateError on duplicates. Registration now lives in a single effect keyed on user id, with a module-level registry that unregisters before re-registering. Accomplishments A user with only a domain name gets uptime monitoring, DNS checks, and cert-expiry monitoring by typing one sentence. Zero duplicated tool definitions between the hosted MCP connector and the in-page WebMCP surface, as we using same manifest for both to avoid drift between them. A human in the loop on every write without adding a single new backend endpoint or permission model. The public free tools work with ChatGPT for anyone, no account, no API key. What we learned Agent traffic is one more client of the API you already have. If tenant scoping and authorisation live server-side, WebMCP costs little to add and adds no new attack surface. If they live in the UI, the agent will reach things it should not. Tool descriptions are very important and needs to explain what it is. The model picks tools by reading them. "List monitors" performed badly compared to a sentence explaining when to use it and what comes back. This becomes more important with more tools you add. readOnlyHint matters. Without it the agent asked for confirmation on every read and the experience felt slower than clicking. Backend MCP covers automation with no human present. WebMCP covers the person already on the page. What's next We'll expose on-call and escalation tools in-page (who is on call, override a shift, page a person). get_current_view() and navigate_to() so the agent can reason about what the user is looking at. live_observation.first_impression: A polished AlertKick marketing page presents agent-operated monitoring, on-call rosters, escalation, and related monitoring products.
live_observation.after_state: The page navigated/positioned into the product explanation flow, with monitoring and escalation content visible.
live_observation.notes: The public landing page was reachable, but the central monitor-creation workflow appears to require Start free or an authenticated product surface.
